questions.stem: Your squad is six weeks into building a rollout tool for a fibre-to-the-premises programme. In standups one engineer agrees with whatever the team settles on, then messages you privately within the hour setting out why it will not work. He has been right twice. Asked about it, he says he does not want to slow the meeting down or embarrass anyone. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask him to put the objection to the team himself, and back him visibly the first time he does.
options.rationale: The reasoning has to reach the people making the decision, and the only thing standing in the way is the cost he attaches to speaking. Backing him the first time is what lowers that cost for everyone watching.

options.text: Keep taking his messages and raise the points yourself in the standup without naming him.
options.rationale: It preserves the pattern by making it work. You become the channel for one person's dissent, and the team never sees that disagreeing in the room is survivable.

options.text: Thank him and confirm that private messages are the right route, so standups stay short.
options.rationale: This optimises for the length of the meeting over the quality of the decision taken in it. Standups are short because they are focused, not because objections are held back.

options.text: Raise it at the retrospective as a general point about speaking up, without reference to him.
options.rationale: A general prompt gives nobody a specific thing to do differently. He will either not recognise himself in it or recognise himself uncomfortably, and neither outcome changes tomorrow's standup.

questions.explanation: Disagreement that only ever reaches the project manager is not being managed, it is being absorbed. The work is to make dissent cheap at the point where the decision is actually taken, which means lowering the personal cost of the first objection rather than building a private route around it. A team that cannot contradict itself in the open will keep producing unanimous decisions that nobody defends afterwards.
questions.mindset: Make disagreement cheap where the decision is made, rather than becoming the route around it.

questions.stem: Three weeks ago you facilitated a meeting between the mechanical and electrical supervisors at a cement works about who isolates equipment during the annual kiln shutdown. They left the room agreeing a sequence. This morning the argument restarted from the beginning, each describing what was agreed differently, and neither able to point to anything written down. The shutdown begins in nine days. What should the project manager do first?

options.text: Reconvene the two of them, settle the sequence again, and record what was decided, who it binds and when it is reviewed.
options.rationale: The first agreement failed because nothing carried it out of the room. Recording the decision with an owner and a review point is what makes the second one survive contact with the shutdown.

options.text: Decide the isolation sequence yourself and issue it, given how little time is left.
options.rationale: It buys nine days of quiet at the cost of the two people who have to work the sequence never owning it. The next boundary question between these teams now arrives at your desk by default.

options.text: Ask each supervisor to write down his version of the agreement so you can compare them.
options.rationale: This treats the problem as faulty memory when it is an absent decision record. It produces two competing written accounts, which is further from a settlement than the verbal agreement was.

options.text: Escalate to the plant manager on the grounds that both men have failed to hold an agreement.
options.rationale: It reframes a process failure as a discipline problem. Nothing was written down for them to hold to, so the escalation asks the plant manager to sanction people for a gap you own.

questions.explanation: An agreement that exists only in the recollection of the parties will drift, and it drifts fastest under pressure, because each party reconstructs it in the direction of their own interest without any dishonesty. What converts a settlement into something durable is an artefact: the decision, the people it binds, and the date it gets tested. The absence of that artefact is a project management omission rather than a failure of goodwill.
questions.mindset: A settlement that leaves no trace will be re-argued, so give every agreement something that outlives the meeting.

questions.stem: Your programme has put a new job-dispatch system into a vehicle breakdown service. The control room is measured on average time to allocate a job; the roadside technicians are measured on first-visit fix rate. Since go-live the two groups have argued every week: control allocates the nearest van, and technicians say they arrive without the parts they need. Each group is doing exactly what it is measured on. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Take the conflict between the two measures to the director who owns both, since neither group can change its own targets.
options.rationale: The dispute is manufactured by two targets that cannot both be maximised, and neither party has the authority to alter that. It belongs with the person who set both measures.

options.text: Bring both groups together to describe the trade-off in terms of the outcome for the stranded customer.
options.rationale: It reframes an argument between two departments as a shared question about the same customer, which is the only frame in which either group's measure can be judged as too narrow.

options.text: Ask the control room to allocate on parts availability rather than proximity.
options.rationale: It picks a winner and moves the failure to the other measure, where it will surface as a complaint from control instead. Choosing a side in a structural conflict relocates it rather than resolving it.

options.text: Add a rule to the system preventing allocation to any van without the required parts.
options.rationale: This automates around a governance problem and hides the evidence of it. The incompatible targets remain, and the argument reappears as complaints that the system is blocking allocations.

options.text: Run a facilitated workshop on communication between the two groups.
options.rationale: It treats a conflict manufactured by incentives as an interpersonal one. Better communication between two people paid to pull in opposite directions produces a more articulate argument, not fewer of them.

questions.explanation: Where two groups in dispute are each behaving rationally against their own measures, the conflict is a property of the measurement system rather than of the people, and no amount of relationship work will shift it. The diagnostic question is whether either party could concede and still meet the target it is held to. If neither can, the resolution sits with whoever owns both targets, and the project manager's job is to route it there with the trade-off made explicit.
questions.mindset: Before treating a dispute as interpersonal, check whether either side could concede and still hit the number they are judged on.

questions.stem: You have facilitated eleven retrospectives for a team building water-quality monitoring for a salmon farm. Nobody has ever disagreed in one. Actions are agreed unanimously and roughly half of them get done. The last three sprints have each missed their goal, and in one-to-ones people describe obstacles they have never once mentioned in the room. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Gather observations from each person before the next session, publish them unattributed, and open by working through the ones that contradict each other.
options.rationale: It puts the disagreement in the room without requiring anyone to be the first to voice it. Starting from contradictions already on the wall changes the session's default from confirming to examining.

options.text: Ask the team directly in the next retrospective why nobody ever disagrees.
options.rationale: It asks a group that has learned not to speak candidly to explain its own silence, in the very setting where the silence occurs. The likely answer is a polite denial that closes the subject.

options.text: Treat the unanimity as evidence of a cohesive team and tackle the missed sprint goals separately.
options.rationale: It reads absence of conflict as agreement. Eleven sessions without a single disagreement, alongside obstacles raised privately, is evidence that the disagreement has moved somewhere you cannot see it.

options.text: Stop attending the retrospectives so the team can speak more freely.
options.rationale: It assumes your presence is the cause without any evidence for that, and it gives up the ability to hear and act on what is said. If the silence has another cause, you have now removed your only view of it.

questions.explanation: Unanimity is data, and in a team that is missing its goals it is usually bad data. A retrospective's value comes entirely from surfacing the differences between how people experienced the same sprint, so a format that only ever produces consensus has stopped doing its job whatever it feels like in the room. The practical lever is the mechanics of the session rather than an appeal for candour, because format changes who has to go first.
questions.mindset: Read the absence of disagreement as a finding to investigate, not a sign of health.

questions.stem: Three disputes on your rail depot refurbishment have hardened into fixed demands, and each party has stopped explaining why. For each stated position below, identify the underlying interest the party is actually protecting, because that is what any workable settlement has to satisfy. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: The signalling contractor insists on exclusive possession of the depot for the whole of August.
The train operator insists that no work at all takes place between 05:00 and 09:00 on a weekday.
The safety manager insists on being personally present at every heavy lift, which is delaying several of them.

options.text: Certainty that specialist crews booked months in advance are not left standing while access is arranged.
options.rationale: The demand is for a block of time, but what is being protected is the cost of idle specialists. A settlement that guarantees access windows reliably can satisfy that without the whole of August.

options.text: Protection of the morning peak service against which the operator's own performance regime penalises it.
options.rationale: The hours named are not arbitrary, they are the hours the operator is financially measured on. Any settlement has to leave that exposure covered, which is a narrower requirement than a blanket ban.

options.text: Personal accountability for an assurance that his licence does not permit him to delegate.
options.rationale: This looks like an unwillingness to trust colleagues but is a constraint he did not choose and cannot trade away. Relief comes from a second competent licence holder, not from persuading him to relax.

options.text: A wish to demonstrate authority over the other parties working on the site.
options.rationale: Not used. Attributing a fixed position to ego is the standard failure of interest-based analysis, because it is unfalsifiable and it makes the other party the problem. Each demand here has a concrete interest behind it.

questions.explanation: A hardened position is a demand for one particular solution, and it conceals the interest that made that solution attractive. Positions conflict far more often than interests do, which is why settlements become available as soon as the parties are working on what they need rather than what they asked for. The discipline is to keep asking what a demand protects, and to resist the shortcut of explaining an inconvenient position by the character of the person holding it.
questions.mindset: Ask what a fixed demand is protecting, because positions collide far more often than the interests beneath them.

questions.stem: Six weeks ago you decided that a university's admissions replacement would migrate historic applicant data in a single pass rather than two, over the stated objection of the data manager. She has now written to the programme board saying the decision was taken without adequate analysis and that you dismissed her concerns because they were inconvenient. The board has asked you to respond. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Ask the board to appoint someone independent to review the decision on its merits, and give them the analysis and her objection in full.
options.rationale: You are a party to this dispute, so you cannot also be the one who determines whether it was handled fairly. Handing the question to someone independent is what makes either outcome credible to both of you.

options.text: Respond to the board with the analysis demonstrating that the single-pass decision was sound.
options.rationale: It answers the technical charge and ignores the procedural one. A party's own account of its own fairness settles nothing, even when the underlying decision turns out to have been correct.

options.text: Meet her privately first and try to persuade her to withdraw the letter.
options.rationale: Approaching someone privately to retract a concern she raised through a legitimate route looks like pressure, whatever the intention. It contaminates the process and hands her a second, stronger grievance.

options.text: Accept the criticism, reopen the decision and re-run the analysis with her involved.
options.rationale: It treats an allegation of bias as proof that the decision was wrong. Conceding on the strength of the complaint rather than the argument teaches the programme that this route works regardless of merit.

questions.explanation: When a project manager becomes a party to the conflict, the roles of participant and arbiter separate and cannot be recombined. Two distinct questions are now live, whether the decision was right and whether it was reached fairly, and only the first is about the data. Handing the second to someone with no stake in it protects the decision if it was sound and protects the complainant if it was not, which is precisely why it has to be someone else.
questions.mindset: Once you are a party to the dispute, you cannot be the one who judges whether you handled it fairly.

questions.stem: A designer and a back-end developer on your charity fundraising platform disagree about how failed donation attempts should be shown to donors. For eight days the argument has run entirely by email, and every message copies you and the head of digital. The two have not spoken to each other directly once. This morning's message asks you to confirm which of them is right. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Get the two of them into one conversation together, and say plainly that you will not be settling this by email.
options.rationale: Eight days of copied messages is a dispute that has never actually met. Putting them in one conversation removes the audience they have been performing to and makes them address each other.

options.text: Reply to all with your decision, since the question needs settling and they have asked you.
options.rationale: It answers the question that was asked and confirms the method that produced it. Every future disagreement now begins with a message copying you, because that is what worked.

options.text: Reply privately to each of them with your view of the right answer.
options.rationale: It keeps you as the channel and gives two people separate accounts of the same decision, which are guaranteed to differ in emphasis and to be quoted back at each other later.

options.text: Ask the head of digital to rule on it, as the senior person already copied in.
options.rationale: It escalates a two-person design disagreement to a level that neither needs it nor should absorb it, and it rewards the copying by delivering exactly the authority it was fishing for.

questions.explanation: Being copied into a disagreement is a request to become its mechanism, and answering the request is what installs you. A dispute conducted through an intermediary never has to be worked through by the people holding it, so the positions harden while the relationship that would resolve them is never used. Changing the medium is usually the whole intervention, because most of what makes written conflict intractable is the audience and the permanence.
questions.mindset: When a disagreement arrives copied to you, treat the channel as the problem before the content.

questions.stem: A steel fabrication package on your project has an outstanding decision about connection detailing. The two engineers responsible have disagreed for 15 working days and neither will move. The activity waiting on the decision sits on the second-longest path and carries 8 working days of total float. Work out what the disagreement has already cost the completion date, then identify what should have been monitored from the first day.

blanks.label: Working days of delay to project completion, assuming the decision is taken today
blanks.rationale: Fifteen days of delay against eight days of total float leaves seven days with nothing to absorb them, so seven days come straight off the completion date. Float postpones the consequence, it does not remove it.

blanks.label: Working day on which the float was fully consumed
blanks.rationale: The float ran out on day eight, and every day of argument after that converted a local disagreement into project delay. Nothing visible changed on that day, which is exactly why it passes unnoticed.

blanks.label: What the project manager should have been tracking from day one to know when this disagreement became a schedule issue
blanks.rationale: Tracking float consumption is what turns an open disagreement into a dated deadline for resolving it, because it tells you the day on which discussion stops being free.

questions.explanation: Unresolved disagreements consume float silently, and float is the only thing standing between a local argument and a dated commitment. Because nothing visible happens on the day it runs out, a dispute that felt tolerable on Friday is a delay on Monday without anyone deciding anything. Giving a disagreement a resolution date derived from the schedule, rather than from patience, is what puts the cost in front of the parties while there is still something to protect.
questions.mindset: Give every open disagreement a decision date taken from the schedule, because float runs out without announcing itself.

questions.stem: You manage a programme rolling out revised collection rounds for a council's waste contractor. The contractor's operations director, unhappy with your position on the number of vehicles required, has written directly to your sponsor. Your sponsor forwarded the message to you asking why it had reached him. You had been working the issue and had a meeting with the operations director booked for Thursday. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Brief the sponsor on where the issue stands and what you are doing about it, then raise the route directly with the operations director and agree how disagreements will be raised in future.
options.rationale: The sponsor needs the substance so he is not holding an issue with no answer, and the operations director needs the channel addressed by you rather than by the sponsor. Both parts are needed and neither substitutes for the other.

options.text: Tell the sponsor the escalation was premature and ask him to redirect it back to you.
options.rationale: It makes the reply entirely about the breach of channel and leaves the sponsor holding a live complaint with nothing to say about it. He asked why it reached him, not who was at fault.

options.text: Concede the vehicle numbers so that the source of the escalation disappears.
options.rationale: It settles a technical question by reference to who complained loudest and to whom. The contractor now knows the price of going over your head, and will pay it again.

options.text: Raise the operations director's conduct with the contractor's account manager as a relationship issue.
options.rationale: It converts a substantive disagreement about vehicle numbers into a complaint about behaviour, which settles nothing and puts the contractor's commercial team on the defensive before Thursday.

questions.explanation: An escalation past you raises two separate matters, the issue itself and the route it travelled, and collapsing them into one response resolves neither. The sponsor's need is information: what the disagreement is, what is being done, and by when. The route is yours to address with the person who took it, because if the sponsor polices the channel then the channel now runs through the sponsor permanently.
questions.mindset: Answer the substance to whoever received it, and address the route with whoever chose it.

questions.stem: In your team's refinement sessions, one senior developer speaks first and at length on every item, and the team has drifted into agreeing with him. Two quieter members have stopped offering estimates at all, and one told you privately that she sees no point. His technical judgement is usually sound and the team's delivery is currently fine. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Change the mechanics so that views are formed before they are spoken, such as estimating privately then revealing together, and rotating who speaks first.
options.rationale: It addresses the sequencing that causes the anchoring rather than the person doing it, so the team keeps his judgement while recovering the independent views it has been losing.

options.text: Ask him privately to hold back and let other people speak first.
options.rationale: It makes one person's self-restraint the mechanism for a structural problem, which lasts about three sessions. It also costs the team the contribution of its most experienced member to fix a problem he is not solely causing.

options.text: Take no action while his judgement is sound and delivery is unaffected.
options.rationale: It measures the cost only in delivered work. What has been lost is the challenge to an estimate that nobody now tests, and that loss becomes visible only on the item where his judgement is wrong.

options.text: Encourage the quieter members to be more assertive in the sessions.
options.rationale: It puts the burden of changing the dynamic on the people with the least standing to change it, and asks them to take a personal risk to fix a problem in how the session is run.

questions.explanation: When one voice consistently goes first, the rest of the group is estimating against an anchor rather than against the work, and the resulting consensus carries far less information than it appears to. Because the cause is the order in which views are expressed, the reliable fix is procedural rather than personal, and procedural fixes have the advantage that nobody has to be told they are the problem. Silence in a group with an obvious anchor should be read as suppressed information, not agreement.
questions.mindset: When one voice anchors the room, change the order in which views are given rather than asking people to be braver.

questions.stem: Your terminal automation programme changes crane operators' shift patterns at a container port. The works council has formally objected, stating that it was not consulted as the recognition agreement requires, and has asked for the change to be held. Your sponsor tells you the berth commissioning window cannot move and instructs you to proceed. Commissioning is in five weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Set out for the sponsor, in writing, what proceeding without the required consultation exposes the organisation to and what holding the shift change alone would cost, start the consultation in parallel, and leave the choice with him.
options.rationale: The decision is the sponsor's, but it is only his to take once he can see both sides of it. Starting consultation immediately also shortens the very delay he is trying to avoid, whichever way he decides.

options.text: Proceed as instructed and record the sponsor's decision and the works council's objection in the risk register.
options.rationale: It treats a documented instruction as a discharge of responsibility. Recording an exposure is not managing it, and the consultation obligation belongs to the organisation rather than being the sponsor's to waive on request.

options.text: Hold the shift change on your own authority until the consultation has been completed.
options.rationale: It takes a decision that belongs to the sponsor, and takes it by removing his choice rather than informing it. Being right about the obligation does not transfer the authority to act on it unilaterally.

options.text: Ask the works council to accept a retrospective consultation once commissioning is complete.
options.rationale: It asks the aggrieved party to waive the very process whose omission is their grievance, and it does so from the position of someone who needs their agreement. Refusal is near certain and hardens the objection.

questions.explanation: When an instruction from a sponsor collides with an obligation the organisation carries, the project manager neither absorbs the conflict silently nor resolves it by fiat. The obligation is not the sponsor's personal property to trade against a date, so the task is to convert an instruction given without full information into a decision taken with it, and to keep working the underlying constraint while that happens. Escalating a choice upward is not refusing to act.
questions.mindset: When an instruction collides with an obligation, make the choice visible to whoever owns it rather than absorbing it or overruling it.

questions.stem: A pension administration programme is jointly owned by the finance director and the operations director. Your scheme migration lead and the operations lead have been deadlocked for three weeks over whether member records are cleansed before or after migration, and each has their own director's backing. Both directors have told you separately that they would rather not overrule the other. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Put the decision to both directors in the same room, with the cost and date consequences of each option worked out.
options.rationale: Two people avoiding a decision separately will keep avoiding it separately. Together, with the consequences quantified, the cost of not deciding becomes visible to both at once.

options.text: Set a date after which the deadlock itself carries a consequence, such as a stated default taking effect or the plan being rebaselined.
options.rationale: Deadlock persists while it is free. Attaching a dated consequence turns indefinite deferral into a choice someone has to make, without requiring either director to concede to the other first.

options.text: Ask each director separately to concede the point in the interests of the programme.
options.rationale: Sequential private lobbying produces a settlement that neither party watched the other agree to, so each suspects the other was leaned on. It also lets both continue to avoid the conversation they need to have.

options.text: Escalate to the chief executive for a ruling.
options.rationale: It skips the level that is perfectly able to decide and spends significant credibility on a question two directors could settle in twenty minutes. It also tells both of them you found them unusable.

options.text: Leave the two leads to keep negotiating, since they understand the technical detail best.
options.rationale: Three weeks of deadlock is the evidence that this is not about detail. Neither lead has the authority to concede their own director's position, so more negotiation between them cannot produce a decision.

questions.explanation: A deadlock between parties who each have separate backing is a dispute about authority wearing the clothes of a technical disagreement, and it will not yield to more analysis by the people holding the positions. The two moves that work are to assemble the people who can actually decide, and to give the deadlock a cost so that deferral stops being the comfortable option. Neither requires anyone to be shown to have lost.
questions.mindset: When a deadlock survives good arguments, stop supplying arguments and start supplying a decision point.

questions.stem: Two scientists on your crop-genetics data team argue hard in refinement about experimental design. The arguments are about the work rather than about each other, and the stories that come out of them are noticeably better specified. Three other team members have separately asked you to stop the arguing, saying the sessions have become uncomfortable to sit through. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Name the distinction openly with the whole team: disagreement about the work is wanted, and say what would make it unacceptable.
options.rationale: The three who complained cannot currently tell the difference between rigour and hostility, and nobody has told them where the line is. Stating it protects the argument and reassures the audience in the same move.

options.text: Manage the form of the argument rather than its existence, by timeboxing it and requiring a recorded decision at the end.
options.rationale: Much of the discomfort comes from an argument that appears unbounded and inconclusive. Bounding it in time and ending it with a decision changes how it feels without removing what it produces.

options.text: Ask the two scientists to settle their differences before the session so refinement runs smoothly.
options.rationale: It removes from view the reasoning the rest of the team learns from, and leaves them receiving conclusions they cannot interrogate. Smoothness is bought with the team's understanding of its own design decisions.

options.text: Rule on the experimental design yourself so the discomfort ends.
options.rationale: It buys comfort with decision quality, and does so on a technical question where two specialists are better placed than you. The team also learns that visible disagreement gets taken away from them.

options.text: Move refinement to a smaller group of the two scientists plus you.
options.rationale: It resolves the audience's discomfort by shrinking the team's involvement in its own work. The argument continues, but now three people are excluded from the decisions rather than merely uneasy about them.

questions.explanation: Disagreement about the work and disagreement about people look similar from the outside and behave completely differently, and a team that cannot tell them apart will suppress both. Task conflict is worth protecting because it is where the quality comes from, so the intervention is to make the distinction explicit and to manage the form the argument takes. Removing the argument to restore comfort trades something valuable for something that only feels valuable.
questions.mindset: Protect argument about the work while being explicit about where it stops being about the work.

questions.stem: A laboratory technician on your blood service cold-chain traceability project asks whether she can tell you something in confidence and, before you can answer, describes a colleague repeatedly overriding a temperature alarm to avoid the paperwork a breach generates. She then asks you to promise not to act on it, saying she has to work alongside him every day. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Tell her plainly that you cannot hold this in confidence, explain what you are obliged to do with it, and be specific about what you can control in how it is handled.
options.rationale: It is honest about a promise you were never able to give and gives her the one thing that is actually available: influence over how the matter proceeds rather than whether it does.

options.text: Promise confidence, then raise the alarm overrides as though you had noticed them yourself.
options.rationale: It keeps an impossible promise by deceiving her, and the deception will not survive the first investigation. Anyone watching learns that telling you something has unpredictable and concealed consequences.

options.text: Keep the confidence and encourage her to report it herself through the proper channel.
options.rationale: It transfers a patient-safety obligation to the least powerful person involved, and makes acting on it conditional on her willingness to accept a risk you were unwilling to take.

options.text: Tell her the conversation never took place and ask her to put the allegation in writing instead.
options.rationale: It raises the cost of speaking up at the exact moment someone has, and it is transparently an attempt to acquire deniability rather than to resolve a safety problem.

questions.explanation: Confidence cannot be granted before its contents are known, which is why the answer to a request for it is a description of the limits rather than a yes. Once information touches safety or regulatory obligation, the choice about whether to act has already been made by something outside the relationship, and pretending otherwise trades a real obligation for a temporary comfort. What remains genuinely negotiable is the handling: sequence, attribution, and what protection the person raising it gets.
questions.mindset: Say what you can and cannot hold before hearing it, because a promise of confidence made in ignorance is one you will have to break.

questions.stem: Two members of your community solar project disagree about whether the weekly progress note should go out on a Thursday afternoon or a Friday morning. Each has a reasonable argument, neither has a commitment to a stakeholder behind their preference, and the choice can be reversed at any point at no cost. They have brought the disagreement to you to settle. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hand it back: ask them to pick one between themselves, run with it for a month, and change it if it turns out badly.
options.rationale: The cost of being wrong is one week of a progress note, which is far less than the cost of establishing that reversible choices come to you. Trying it is also cheaper than analysing it.

options.text: Decide it yourself, since it takes ten seconds and they have asked.
options.rationale: Cheap once, expensive as a precedent. Every reversible low-stakes choice now has a route to your desk, and the team loses the practice of settling anything without you.

options.text: Run a short facilitated session to explore the reasoning on both sides properly.
options.rationale: It spends structured facilitation, and everyone's time, on a decision whose worst outcome is a note sent on the wrong day. Proportion is part of judgement.

options.text: Ask the sponsor which day she would prefer to receive it.
options.rationale: It escalates a decision that nobody above the team needs to hold, and it teaches the team that even trivial internal disagreements get referred upward.

questions.explanation: The effort spent resolving a disagreement should be proportionate to the cost of getting it wrong, and reversible low-stakes choices are where a team learns to settle things for itself. Taking those decisions on, however quick they are, trains people to bring the next one too, and the habit is much easier to establish than to undo. Where a decision can be tested cheaply, trying it beats analysing it.
questions.mindset: Match the effort of resolution to the cost of being wrong, and give reversible decisions back to the people making them.

questions.stem: After a long disagreement about whether to automate the batch-record checks on a distillery bottling line, your team lead said in the meeting that he accepted the decision. Since then he has done precisely what was agreed and nothing beyond it: no suggestions, no problems raised, and he has twice referred to it in front of the team as 'your approach'. Sprint output is unchanged. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Talk to him, describe what you have observed without accusation, and find out what he did not say in the meeting.
options.rationale: The observable behaviour is specific enough to describe and ambiguous enough to need explaining, and the reasoning he withheld is exactly what you wanted him in the room for.

options.text: Accept it as compliance and monitor delivery for any actual impact.
options.rationale: It mistakes the absence of obstruction for agreement. The cost is not in this sprint's output but in the problems he can see coming and has decided are no longer his to mention.

options.text: Reopen the decision so that he can be brought along properly.
options.rationale: Reopening a settled decision on the strength of someone's mood rather than a new argument teaches the team that quiet withdrawal is an effective way to reverse things they lost.

options.text: Praise him publicly for supporting the decision despite having argued against it.
options.rationale: It rewards the appearance of agreement and makes the unstated objection much harder to raise, since he would now be contradicting the praise as well as the decision.

questions.explanation: Saying yes in the room is not the same as commitment, and the difference shows up in discretionary effort rather than in compliance. Genuine disagree-and-commit is explicit on both halves, so the person says what they still think is wrong and then acts wholeheartedly anyway. Silent compliance keeps the objection intact and unavailable, which means the project loses the early warning that the objection contained.
questions.mindset: Treat commitment as something stated out loud, because silent compliance keeps the objection and withholds the warning.

questions.stem: You take over a canal restoration project. Two years ago your predecessor settled a dispute between the volunteer heritage group and the engineering contractor by ruling that the contractor's method statements take precedence in every case. The ruling is documented and has held since. In practice the volunteers now raise almost every issue as a complaint about that ruling, and the contractor cites it to avoid discussing anything. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat the ruling itself as the live source of conflict, and reopen it as a question about how the two parties work together rather than about which one prevails.
options.rationale: A settlement that has to be re-cited weekly is not holding, it is being enforced. Reopening on the process rather than the outcome gives both parties something to gain from the conversation.

options.text: Reaffirm the ruling, since it is properly documented and the project has kept moving under it.
options.rationale: It mistakes the absence of open conflict for resolution. A settlement one side re-litigates through every other issue has converted a single dispute into a permanent friction.

options.text: Reverse it in the volunteers' favour to restore goodwill with the heritage group.
options.rationale: It swaps which party is aggrieved and establishes that the rule changes with the project manager, which invites the contractor to wait for the next one.

options.text: Ask both parties to bring future issues to you rather than referring back to the ruling.
options.rationale: It makes you the permanent workaround for a settlement that does not work, and the volume of issues means that role will consume you rather than reduce the conflict.

questions.explanation: A resolution that requires an authority to be invoked each time it is applied has suppressed a dispute rather than settled it, and suppression accumulates. The diagnostic signal is not whether the parties comply but whether the ruling still has to do the work: if one side quotes it to avoid discussion and the other treats every issue as an appeal against it, the underlying disagreement is fully intact. Inherited settlements deserve the same test as new ones.
questions.mindset: A settlement that must be quoted to be obeyed has suppressed the dispute rather than resolved it.

questions.stem: On your quarry weighbridge replacement, two people have each missed the same agreed evidence deadlines three times and have each been sharp with the site clerk when challenged about it. One is an employee of your organisation; the other is a contractor engaged through an agency. A team member has asked you why you appear to be dealing with one of them and not the other. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Hold both to the same standard on the project while using the correct route for each, line management for one and the agency and contract manager for the other, and tell the team that this is what is happening.
options.rationale: It keeps the standard identical and the mechanism appropriate, and it answers the fairness question that was actually asked rather than leaving the team to infer an answer.

options.text: Handle both through your own line manager so that the treatment is demonstrably consistent.
options.rationale: It puts consistency of route above correctness of route. Your line manager has no authority over an agency worker, so the process would be both ineffective and improper.

options.text: Raise both cases with the agency and the employee's manager in a single message so nothing looks hidden.
options.rationale: It shares individual conduct information across two employers who have no right to each other's personnel matters, and transparency to the wrong audience is not fairness.

options.text: Explain to the team that contractors are handled differently and leave it at that.
options.rationale: It answers the process question and ignores the fairness question, which is the one being asked. The team's concern is that the standard differs, not that the paperwork does.

questions.explanation: Equal standards and identical mechanisms are different things, and conflating them produces either unfairness or impropriety. The behaviour expected on the project applies to everyone working on it regardless of who employs them, while the route for addressing a shortfall follows the employment relationship. Because the routes are invisible from the outside, unexplained difference reads as favouritism, which makes saying what is happening part of the action rather than an optional courtesy.
questions.mindset: Hold one standard for everyone, use the right mechanism for each, and say enough that the difference is not read as favouritism.

questions.stem: The timeline plots a disagreement between two suppliers on your grid connection works across eleven weeks, from an initial difference of view about cable routing through to a formal contractual notice. Four moments are marked, each showing what was observable to you at the time. Select the moment at which the project manager should intervene.

graphic.title: Eleven-week timeline of a supplier disagreement with four observable moments marked
graphic.caption: Select a moment. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between them, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Week 1 — the two site engineers describe the cable route differently in a progress meeting
regions.rationale: A difference of view is not yet a conflict, and intervening here teaches a team to route every disagreement through you. It also removes the chance that two competent engineers settle it themselves, which is the most likely outcome.

regions.label: Week 3 — the engineers stop copying each other and begin copying their commercial managers
regions.rationale: The moment the parties change the audience is the moment the dispute stops being technical. That shift is the earliest reliable signal that it will not resolve itself, and it happens while both positions are still cheap to move.

regions.label: Week 7 — each supplier issues a revised programme showing the other as the cause of delay
regions.rationale: By now both positions are documented and commercially committed, so intervention is still necessary but far more expensive. Each party has something to defend beyond the original question about cable routing.

regions.label: Week 11 — the formal contractual notice arrives
regions.rationale: Waiting for the contractual trigger hands the dispute to a mechanism rather than a manager. The project manager's discretion has been spent, and the process that follows serves entitlement rather than the works.

questions.explanation: Disagreements give off a reliable signal before they harden, and it is a change in audience rather than a change in volume. When parties begin addressing people who can defend them commercially instead of each other, the dispute has been reclassified in their own minds, and every subsequent artefact is built to support a position. Intervening on that signal is cheap; intervening once positions are documented means asking people to abandon something they have committed to in writing.
questions.mindset: Watch for the change in who is being copied, because a dispute changes character before it changes volume.

questions.stem: The diagram shows the responsibility model agreed for your hospital sterile services system after go-live, with three parties and the activities each owns. The same argument has recurred four times in six weeks, always about who acts first when an instrument tray is rejected at ward level. Select the part of the model that is producing the recurring conflict.

graphic.title: Post-go-live responsibility model showing three parties, their activities, one overlap and one gap
graphic.caption: Select a part of the model. Use Tab or the arrow keys to move between parts, then Enter or Space.

regions.label: Supplier — corrective maintenance of the tray tracking hardware
regions.rationale: This activity has a single named owner and has not featured in any of the four arguments. A boundary nobody is disputing is not the one to redraw, however tempting it is to tidy the model while you are in it.

regions.label: Overlap — 'investigate a rejected tray', listed under both the ward team and sterile services
regions.rationale: One activity owned by two parties with no stated order of precedence is the structural cause. Each recurrence is the model working exactly as written, which is why the argument returns however reasonable the individuals are.

regions.label: Ward team — recording the rejection in the tracking system
regions.rationale: A single-owner activity that nobody has contested. Recording the rejection is not the step the four arguments have been about, and changing it would leave the disputed step untouched.

regions.label: Gap — 'trend analysis of rejections', listed under no party at all
regions.rationale: An unowned activity is a genuine defect in the model, but it produces nothing happening rather than two parties colliding. The symptom described is a repeated argument, which points to duplication rather than omission.

questions.explanation: A conflict that recurs at the same boundary with different people each time is a fault in the responsibility model, not a failure of the individuals standing at it. Duplicated ownership and omitted ownership both cause trouble but present differently: duplication produces collision and argument, while omission produces silence and things quietly not done. Reading the symptom tells you which defect you are looking at, and repairing the model is what stops the fifth recurrence.
questions.mindset: When the same argument returns with different people in it, look for the fault in the model rather than in the people.

questions.stem: After two difficult sessions, the crewing manager and the pilots' representative on your airline rostering programme have agreed how standby days will be allocated during the transition. Both said in the room that they can live with it. Your predecessor reached a broadly similar agreement last year which had unravelled within a month. Which two actions should the project manager take now?

options.text: Write down what was decided and what each party is relying on, and send it to both for correction rather than for approval.
options.rationale: Asking for corrections surfaces the divergence in understanding while goodwill is highest, and it records the reliance rather than only the outcome, which is the part that usually turns out to differ.

options.text: Fix a date now, while both are willing, to review whether the arrangement is working in practice.
options.rationale: Agreeing the review while the agreement is fresh removes the need for anyone to ask for one later, which by then would look like a complaint and be resisted as one.

options.text: Ask both parties to sign a formal undertaking to be held to the arrangement.
options.rationale: It raises the ceremony without raising the commitment, and signals distrust at the precise moment goodwill peaks. Formality is not what failed last year; follow-through was.

options.text: Announce the agreement to the wider crew community straight away to build confidence.
options.rationale: Publishing before the parties have checked the wording turns a fragile agreement into a public position each must now defend, which makes the first correction far more costly than it needs to be.

options.text: Keep the arrangement informal so that it can flex as the transition develops.
options.rationale: Last year's unravelling is direct evidence that informality is the failure mode here. Flexibility that nobody has written down is indistinguishable from each party doing what it originally wanted.

questions.explanation: Most agreements fail after the room rather than in it, and they fail in two predictable ways: nothing carries them into the work, and nobody is scheduled to notice when they stop being followed. The countermeasures are unglamorous, being a written record that the parties have had the chance to correct and a review date agreed while everyone is still willing. A history of the same agreement unravelling is a reason to add mechanism, not solemnity.
questions.mindset: Agreements fail after the room, so leave the room with a record the parties have corrected and a date to test it.

questions.stem: Two disagreements in your team ended this week without anyone raising a further objection, and your instinct is to mark both as resolved in your notes. Before you do, it is worth naming what actually happened in each, because an argument that has stopped is not always one that has been settled. Complete each sentence with the response that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: A developer who argued strongly for a different testing approach conceded within a minute of the tech lead disagreeing, and has since raised the same concern to you privately twice. The project manager should treat this as
Two designers who disagreed about the onboarding flow have each moved halfway, producing a design that neither of them believes serves the user well. The project manager should treat this as

options.text: a withdrawal that has left the argument intact, and reopen it where the team can hear the reasoning
options.rationale: A concession that fast, followed by private repetition, means the position was abandoned rather than changed. The reasoning is still live and the only people who have not heard it are the ones who needed to.

options.text: a compromise that has cost the thing both parties were trying to protect, and test it against the user need
options.rationale: Splitting the difference settles the dispute rather than the problem. When both parties think the result is worse than their own proposal, the trade was made on the wrong axis entirely.

options.text: a collaboration that has produced a better answer than either party started with
options.rationale: Not used. Collaboration is recognisable by an outcome both parties consider better than their opening position, and neither situation here has that. One ended in silence and the other in mutual dissatisfaction.

questions.explanation: A disagreement that has stopped is not necessarily a disagreement that has been resolved, and the way it stopped tells you what to do next. Withdrawal preserves the position and removes it from view, compromise can trade away the interest that made the argument worth having, and only collaboration reliably leaves both parties better off than they started. Naming the mode by its outcome, rather than by how peaceful the room became, is what makes the difference visible.
questions.mindset: Judge how a disagreement ended by what the outcome is worth, not by how quiet the room went.

questions.stem: A boundary dispute between your commissioning and operations teams has been re-argued in the weekly coordination meeting for the past nine weeks. Each time it takes about 25 minutes, and eleven people are present throughout. Their average charged rate is £58 an hour. Work out what the unresolved disagreement has cost in meeting time alone, and identify what that figure has to be set against before it can support a decision.

blanks.label: Total person-hours spent re-arguing the dispute across the nine weeks
blanks.rationale: Twenty-five minutes is 0.4167 hours, multiplied by eleven people and nine occurrences gives 41.25 person-hours. The cost accrues per attendee rather than per meeting, which is what makes recurring agenda items so expensive.

blanks.label: Cost of that time in £, to the nearest £10
blanks.rationale: 41.25 person-hours at £58 an hour is £2,392.50, or £2,390 to the nearest ten pounds. Putting a figure on a tolerated irritation is often what finally gets it scheduled as a decision.

blanks.label: What this figure must be compared against before it can justify a particular settlement
blanks.rationale: A cost of delay only argues for action when set against what resolving the matter would cost. On its own it establishes that the argument is expensive, not that any particular answer to it is right.

questions.explanation: Recurring disagreements are usually tolerated because their cost is spread thinly enough to stay invisible, and converting that cost into a single number is often what turns a standing irritation into something with an owner and a date. The number has to be handled honestly, though: it argues for deciding, not for deciding in any particular direction, and using a delay cost to press for one party's preferred outcome is a rhetorical move rather than an analytical one.
questions.mindset: Price the delay to justify making the decision, never to justify which way it goes.

questions.stem: Your installation engineer has twice had a sharp exchange with a textile mill's shift supervisor about access to the dye house. Your engineer says the supervisor blocks him for no reason; the supervisor has complained to the mill's engineering manager that your engineer is arrogant. The mill is your client. As far as you can establish, your engineer's account of the access delays is accurate. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Separate the two questions: take the access constraint to the client's engineering manager as a project issue, and deal with your engineer's manner with your engineer.
options.rationale: The delays and the conduct are independent problems with different owners, and each becomes solvable once it is not being used to answer the other.

options.text: Defend your engineer to the client, since his account of the access delays is demonstrably accurate.
options.rationale: It offers accuracy about the facts as a defence of the manner, which is not what was complained about. It also spends client relationship on a point you could have won through the engineering manager anyway.

options.text: Instruct your engineer to avoid the supervisor and route all access requests through you.
options.rationale: It removes the friction by removing the working relationship, and makes you a permanent relay for a site you are not on. The two still have to work together the moment you are unavailable.

options.text: Ask the client to address the access delays with their supervisor before you do anything else.
options.rationale: It leads with a complaint about their staff while your own conduct issue sits unaddressed, and the client already has an account in which your engineer is the problem.

questions.explanation: Being right about the substance does not settle a question about conduct, and running the two together lets each side dismiss the half that is inconvenient. Handled separately, an access constraint is a legitimate project issue for the client's management chain and a sharp manner is a legitimate matter for your own. Handled together, the client hears excuses and your engineer hears that his behaviour is acceptable whenever his facts are good.
questions.mindset: Being right about the facts is never an answer to a question about conduct.

questions.stem: Your mortgage servicing migration has two streams, and their leads have argued for a fortnight about which gets the two available test analysts. Each has a strong case. Reviewing the correspondence, you notice that you have told both streams they are on the critical path, at different times and in different forums. Neither lead has mentioned this to you. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Say plainly that the priority between the streams was never actually set, set it now, and tell both leads that the argument was a consequence of that.
options.rationale: It fixes the cause rather than the instance, and naming your own part is what stops both leads reading the eventual decision as a judgement on their case.

options.text: Allocate the analysts by comparing the two business cases on their merits.
options.rationale: It settles this instance by a defensible method while leaving in place the condition that produced it. Two streams both told they come first will generate the next contest over the next scarce resource.

options.text: Split the analysts, one to each stream.
options.rationale: An even split looks even-handed and meets neither stream's need. It also avoids stating a priority, which is the specific thing that is missing.

options.text: Ask the two leads to reach agreement between themselves, offering to arbitrate if they cannot.
options.rationale: It delegates a decision they are not equipped to make, because the information they lack is yours. They will negotiate energetically from two premises that cannot both be true.

questions.explanation: Two capable people arguing reasonably and irreconcilably is often a sign that someone above them has supplied both premises, and the resource in dispute is merely where the ambiguity became visible. Before treating a contest over people or equipment as a dispute between the claimants, it is worth checking what each of them has been told, because a conflict manufactured by unclear priority cannot be resolved by whoever is currently holding it. Owning the ambiguity publicly is part of removing it.
questions.mindset: When two reasonable people cannot agree, check whether they are arguing from premises you gave them.

questions.stem: Six weeks ago a senior ranger applied for the product owner role on your national park visitor-management project and was not appointed. Since then she has missed three workshops, questioned the appointed product owner's decisions in front of others, and told two colleagues that the process had been decided in advance. Her operational knowledge is the best available and the project needs it. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Speak to her directly, acknowledge the appointment as the obvious context, be specific about what the project needs and what is not workable, and settle whether she is in or out.
options.rationale: Nothing has yet been named to her, so she has had no opportunity to change. Naming the cause and the behaviour together is what turns a drift into a choice she has to make.

options.text: Work around her by getting the operational detail from other rangers instead.
options.rationale: It accepts the loss of the best available knowledge and lets the behaviour stand as the price of avoiding one conversation. Others watching learn what obstruction costs, which is nothing.

options.text: Raise it with her line manager as a performance matter.
options.rationale: It routes to a formal process something that has never been put to her informally. Escalating before the conversation removes the cheapest route to resolution and makes the grievance concrete.

options.text: Give her a defined role alongside the product owner so she is visibly involved.
options.rationale: It rewards obstruction with status and installs a second centre of authority beside the person just appointed, which undermines the appointment you are trying to protect.

questions.explanation: Behaviour that follows a disappointment is usually about the disappointment, and it persists while everyone politely pretends not to see the connection. A grievance that has never been named cannot be resolved, so the conversation that acknowledges the cause is also the one that makes a choice possible for the person holding it. That conversation has to carry both halves, the acknowledgement and the boundary, because either alone reads as insincere.
questions.mindset: Name the cause and the boundary in the same conversation, because a grievance nobody will mention cannot be settled.

questions.stem: Halfway through your ERP rollout at a ceramics manufacturer, the company announces that two of its three plants will merge their planning functions. Your project team includes people from both. Within a week, meetings have become guarded, two members have stopped sharing data with each other, and a decision that was settled in March has been reopened. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Name openly with the team what has changed, and say what you do and do not know about how it affects them.
options.rationale: The guardedness is being driven by a question nobody will say out loud. Saying it out loud, including the parts you cannot answer, removes the need for each person to fill the silence privately.

options.text: Separate project decisions from the reorganisation by establishing which decisions are unaffected by it, and confirming those.
options.rationale: It shrinks the area of genuine uncertainty and stops the reorganisation being used, consciously or not, to reopen anything a party dislikes.

options.text: Ask the team to set the reorganisation aside and concentrate on delivery.
options.rationale: It instructs people to stop feeling the thing that is actually driving their behaviour, which produces compliance in the meeting and no change outside it.

options.text: Escalate the data-sharing behaviour to the sponsor as a performance concern.
options.rationale: It reads a predictable response to job insecurity as individual failure, and it punishes people for protecting themselves in circumstances the organisation created.

options.text: Pause the project until the reorganisation has been settled.
options.rationale: It converts uncertainty into stoppage on a timetable that is not yours, and restarting will cost more than the disruption you are avoiding.

questions.explanation: When people whose jobs are in question are asked to collaborate, the cooperation that a project depends on becomes personally risky, and the resulting conflict is rational rather than obstructive. What helps is reducing the ambiguity that can be reduced and being honest about the part that cannot, because unstated uncertainty is filled in by each person separately and always pessimistically. Confirming which decisions stand also denies the reorganisation its use as a lever to reopen settled things.
questions.mindset: Under organisational uncertainty, shrink what is unknown and say plainly what remains, rather than asking people to ignore it.

questions.stem: In planning for your fruit-grading software, a developer told the team that the product owner's delivery dates were 'fantasy' and that everyone in the room knew it. The product owner did not respond. The dates in question came from a customer commitment made before the team existed, and the team's own estimates last sprint were exceeded by a wide margin. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Address both parts in the open: that the dates came from a commitment rather than from an estimate, and that describing a colleague's work as fantasy is not how this team disagrees.
options.rationale: The objection contains an accurate point and an unacceptable delivery, and answering only one of them leaves the other looking endorsed. Doing it in the open matters because that is where it happened.

options.text: Address the developer's tone privately and let the dates stand.
options.rationale: It handles the manner and leaves the substance, so an accurate objection about where the dates came from goes unanswered and returns, probably in the same tone.

options.text: Ask the team to re-estimate and revise the dates accordingly.
options.rationale: It acts on the substance while letting the manner pass, which teaches the team that the way to move a date is to say so bluntly in front of everyone.

options.text: Back the product owner publicly to protect her standing with the team.
options.rationale: It defends the person by defending a date you know did not come from the team, which costs you the credibility you will need for the next disagreement about dates.

questions.explanation: Objections frequently arrive as a valid point wrapped in an unacceptable delivery, and responding to only one half signals that the other was fine. The substance here is a real distinction between a commitment inherited from elsewhere and an estimate the team owns, which is worth stating plainly because it changes what the conversation is about. The manner is a separate matter and belongs in the same forum it occurred in, so that the norm is visible to everyone who heard the original remark.
questions.mindset: When an objection is right and badly made, answer both halves, and answer them where it happened.

questions.stem: In today's sprint review for an opticians' booking product, with the client's operations lead present, a developer said that the reason appointment reminders still do not work is that a named colleague 'never finishes anything'. The colleague was sitting in the room. The reminders have genuinely slipped twice. The client's operations lead is now waiting for your response. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Stop it there, say that the reminders will be answered and that individual performance is not discussed in this forum, then deal with both people afterwards.
options.rationale: It draws the line in front of the people who witnessed the breach, which is the only place the norm registers, while deferring the substance and the individual matters to the right settings.

options.text: Answer the substantive point about the reminders and move the review on.
options.rationale: It lets a personal attack stand unremarked in front of a client. Everyone present, including the client, will remember the silence rather than the answer about reminders.

options.text: Invite the named colleague to give his side of it.
options.rationale: It requires the person attacked to defend himself publicly, which compounds the injury and converts the review into the argument it should not host.

options.text: Apologise to the client for the team's conduct and continue with the review.
options.rationale: It manages the client's impression while saying nothing to the people whose behaviour is at issue, so the audience most in need of hearing the standard does not.

questions.explanation: Some things have to be addressed in the moment because the audience is the point: a norm that is only ever enforced privately is invisible to everyone who saw it broken. What can be deferred is the substance and the individual conversations, and separating those from the immediate intervention keeps the response short enough to be proportionate. The client's presence raises the stakes without changing the action, since a team that polices itself in front of a client is more reassuring than one that never slips.
questions.mindset: Enforce the norm in front of the people who saw it broken, and defer everything that can wait.

questions.stem: Over the past quarter, three settlements that were properly reached on your programme have quietly stopped working, and each has failed for a different underlying reason. Match each symptom to the repair that fits it, because applying the wrong repair tends to confirm the parties' suspicion that the original agreement was never worth much. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Both parties describe the agreement accurately and identically, and neither is doing what it says.
The parties are doing exactly what they agreed, and a third team materially affected by it never accepted anything.
Each party is acting on a different understanding of the same words, and both are acting in good faith.

options.text: Attach the agreement to something that follows it up: a named owner and a review date.
options.rationale: Accurate shared recall with no action means nothing carried the agreement into the work. Understanding was never the problem, so restating or clarifying it will change nothing.

options.text: Reopen the agreement with the missing party present as a party rather than as a recipient.
options.rationale: An agreement between the wrong set of people does not bind the ones left out. Informing them afterwards reproduces the original failure with better manners.

options.text: Rewrite the disputed term as a worked example that both parties check against a real case.
options.rationale: Good-faith divergence on identical words is an ambiguity problem, and ambiguity hides in abstractions. A concrete case forces the difference into the open where it can be settled.

options.text: Escalate to the sponsor to impose a decision on the parties.
options.rationale: Not used. Imposition is the remedy for a refusal to agree, and none of these three is a refusal. Each is an agreement that exists and fails for a mechanical reason imposition would not touch.

questions.explanation: Agreements fail in distinguishable ways, and the repair only works if it matches the failure. Non-performance despite shared understanding is a follow-through problem, unaffected parties are a scope-of-agreement problem, and good-faith divergence on the same wording is an ambiguity problem. Reaching for authority is the common reflex and it addresses none of the three, because in each case the parties have already agreed to something. Diagnosing before repairing is what stops a second failed settlement.
questions.mindset: Diagnose how an agreement failed before repairing it, because the wrong repair proves the agreement was worthless.

questions.stem: Your sponsor and the fisheries regulator disagree about whether catch-reporting data must be retained for five years or seven. Your sponsor has told the team to build for five and to let the regulator argue about it afterwards. Your data lead has come to you saying she does not want to build something she may later be asked to justify. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Push the disagreement back to the level that owns it, and meanwhile have the retention period built as a configurable setting rather than an assumption baked into the design.
options.rationale: It refuses to let a design decision silently settle a dispute between two authorities, and it keeps the option open at low cost while the people who can decide do so.

options.text: Build for five years as instructed and record the regulator's position in the risk register.
options.rationale: It puts the team's work behind one party's position in a live dispute and relabels the resulting exposure as a risk, which describes the problem rather than addressing it.

options.text: Build for seven years, since that satisfies both requirements.
options.rationale: It quietly takes the regulator's side and commits cost the sponsor has not agreed, resolving the dispute by concealing it inside a technical decision nobody reviewed.

options.text: Ask the data lead to raise her concern with the sponsor directly.
options.rationale: It sends the least powerful person into a dispute between two authorities that is not hers to settle, and makes her personally responsible for a conflict she only reported.

questions.explanation: When two authorities disagree, the point of danger is that an implementation decision quietly becomes the settlement, after which reversing it is expensive and whoever built it owns the choice. Deferring the commitment, by keeping the contested parameter changeable, buys time without taking sides and costs far less than either party's preferred certainty. The disagreement itself has to go back to the people with standing to resolve it rather than being absorbed by the team.
questions.mindset: Never let a build decision quietly settle a dispute between two authorities: defer the commitment and return the argument.

questions.stem: A two-year disagreement about replanting standards between your silviculture manager and the harvesting contractor's agent ended last month when the agent left the contractor. Your silviculture manager has told the team the matter is now closed and has started applying his own standard. The contractor has said nothing at all. The replanting season begins in three weeks. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Treat the disagreement as still open, and get the standard agreed with the contractor's new representative before the season starts.
options.rationale: The dispute was between two organisations, and only one person left. Settling it now, while there is still time, is cheaper than discovering the contractor's position mid-season.

options.text: Accept the resolution, since neither party is currently contesting anything.
options.rationale: It reads the departure of an individual as the settling of an issue. Silence from an organisation nobody has asked is not consent, and it will end the moment the standard costs the contractor something.

options.text: Ask the silviculture manager to hold off applying his standard until the contractor objects.
options.rationale: It waits for the dispute to resurface at the point when it is most expensive, three weeks into a season with crews mobilised and no time to negotiate.

options.text: Write to the contractor confirming the agreed standard.
options.rationale: It records as agreed a position the contractor never accepted, converting an open disagreement into a documented misunderstanding that will be produced later as evidence of bad faith.

questions.explanation: Agreements and disputes are held by organisations even when they are conducted by individuals, so a change of personnel changes who is holding the position rather than whether it exists. The reflex to treat a departure as a resolution is strong because the friction genuinely stops, but the silence that follows is the absence of a representative rather than the presence of consent. Re-confirming a contested position with the new person is a small cost against a season.
questions.mindset: A dispute belongs to the organisation, so when the person leaves, re-confirm rather than inherit.

questions.stem: Your product team works across Auckland, Kraków and Vancouver, with no hour in which all three are awake. A disagreement about the release-branch policy has run for three weeks in a single comment thread. Each region adds to it overnight, so each morning the others find the argument has moved without them. Positions have hardened and two people have stopped reading the thread. Which two actions should the project manager take?

options.text: Close the thread and move the decision to one synchronous conversation, accepting that two of the three regions will meet at an unsociable hour.
options.rationale: Three weeks of hardening is evidence the medium cannot converge this. The unsociable hour is a real cost, and it is smaller than a fourth week, provided it is shared rather than always imposed on the same region.

options.text: State when the decision will be made and who makes it if the conversation has not converged by then.
options.rationale: An asynchronous argument has no natural end, so it needs one supplied. Naming the decider in advance also stops the outcome looking like whoever posted last or shouted loudest won.

options.text: Let the region with the most affected engineers decide the policy.
options.rationale: It settles by headcount and geography, which are proxies for nothing relevant, and hands two regions a policy they had no part in. The disagreement moves rather than ending.

options.text: Summarise the thread each morning and circulate the summary to all three regions.
options.rationale: It improves the legibility of the mechanism that is causing the problem, and installs you as the daily curator of an argument that still has no way of ending.

options.text: Ask everyone to keep contributions shorter and more factual.
options.rationale: It treats a structural problem with asynchrony as a writing-quality issue, and produces a more concise version of the same unresolvable thread.

questions.explanation: Written asynchronous discussion is a poor medium for convergence because it lacks the two things that end an argument, which are the ability to check understanding in real time and a natural stopping point. Where positions have hardened, no improvement to the thread will resolve it, so the choices are a synchronous conversation at real personal cost or a stated decision point with a named decider. Distributing the inconvenience of the unsociable hour across regions over time is what keeps the remedy usable.
questions.mindset: Asynchronous discussion cannot converge a hardened disagreement, so buy a real-time conversation or set a decision point.

questions.stem: Your programme mailbox receives an unsigned message alleging that one of your team leads has been altering test evidence in order to close defects. The message cites two specific record numbers. You have no idea who sent it. The team lead has an unblemished record, and the programme is four weeks from a service assessment. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Have the two cited records checked through whatever route your organisation uses for allegations of this kind, rather than by approaching him yourself.
options.rationale: The claim is specific and therefore testable regardless of who made it, and using the proper route protects both the integrity of the check and the team lead if it is unfounded.

options.text: Disregard it, since an anonymous allegation cannot be tested.
options.rationale: It treats anonymity as though it settled credibility. Two record numbers can be examined without knowing anything about the sender, and the assessment in four weeks makes disregarding it the more dangerous option.

options.text: Put the allegation to the team lead directly and judge his reaction.
options.rationale: It substitutes demeanour for evidence, which is unreliable in both directions, and if the allegation is false it tells him he was accused on the strength of nothing.

options.text: Ask the team to establish who sent the message before considering its contents.
options.rationale: It puts the source ahead of the substance and converts a checkable claim into a hunt for whoever raised it, which is the fastest way to ensure nothing is ever raised again.
