questions.explanation: An anonymous allegation is assessed on whether it is checkable, not on what can be inferred about the motives of someone whose identity is unknown. Specific, verifiable detail is the feature that makes an allegation actionable, and it also makes it disprovable, which protects the accused as much as it exposes wrongdoing. Pursuing the source instead of the substance both leaves the question open and signals to everyone watching what happens to people who report things.
questions.mindset: Test an allegation on whether it can be checked, not on what you can guess about who made it.

questions.stem: Over a fortnight, four separate matters have been brought to you personally, each by someone who plainly wants you to sort it out, and your instinct is to help with all four. Taking on a dispute that somebody else should be holding is as much a failure as ignoring one, so for each of the following, identify who should own resolving it. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Two developers disagree about how events should be named in the shared schema, and both conventions work.
A team member reports that a colleague has repeatedly made remarks about her accent.
The product owner and the team disagree about whether a partially complete story can be shown at review.
Your team and the platform team disagree about which budget pays for an additional test environment.

options.text: The two developers, with the outcome recorded once as a convention
options.rationale: A reversible technical choice between two workable options is precisely what a team should settle without its project manager. The lasting output is the convention, which prevents the next instance.

options.text: The organisation's formal route for conduct of this kind, started immediately
options.rationale: Alleged discriminatory conduct is not a project disagreement and must not be informally mediated by a project manager, however good the working relationship or however well-meant the intention.

options.text: The team itself, through its own working agreement about what is shown at review
options.rationale: This is a recurring definitional question the team is entitled to settle for itself, and a ruling from you would remove the shared agreement they actually need to hold each other to.

options.text: The two budget holders, with the project manager supplying the cost and the date
options.rationale: Neither team can commit the other's money, so the decision sits with those who can. The project manager's job here is to make the decision decidable rather than to make it.

options.text: The project sponsor, as the ultimate decision-maker on the programme
options.rationale: Not used. Every one of these has a nearer and better-placed owner, and routing all four upward would spend sponsor attention on decisions that three other parties are in a stronger position to take.

questions.explanation: The first question about any disagreement is who owns it, and the answer is frequently not the project manager. Absorbing disputes that belong to a team removes the practice it needs, absorbing ones that turn on funding commits money nobody has given you, and absorbing ones that belong in a formal conduct process is actively harmful to the person who raised it. Correct routing is a substantive act rather than an administrative one.
questions.mindset: Ask who owns a disagreement before asking how to solve it, because taking on the wrong one is its own failure.

questions.stem: A junior analyst on your weather forecasting product devised the anomaly-detection approach that the client praised at last week's showcase. Your tech lead presented it and did not mention her. She has told you she does not want a fuss made and has asked you to leave it alone. Two other team members have separately raised it with you since. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Take attribution up with the tech lead as a team norm, and find a way to correct the record that does not place her at the centre of it.
options.rationale: It respects what she actually asked for, which was not to be made the subject of a scene, while still addressing a norm that two other people have now noticed is missing.

options.text: Leave it, as she has explicitly asked you to.
options.rationale: It treats her wish to avoid discomfort as a decision about the team's standards, which is not hers alone to make. Two colleagues raising it independently shows the effect extends past her.

options.text: Correct the record publicly at the next showcase.
options.rationale: It honours the contribution by overriding her explicit request and making her the focus of exactly the attention she asked to avoid, which teaches her that telling you what she wants achieves nothing.

options.text: Tell the two colleagues who raised it that she has asked for the matter to be dropped.
options.rationale: It shares her position without her consent and closes down the two people who correctly identified a problem, which discourages anyone from mentioning the next one.

questions.explanation: A request not to make a fuss is a request about method rather than a waiver of the underlying issue, and the two can usually be separated. Attribution is a team norm that affects everyone's willingness to contribute visibly, so it survives one person's preference not to be discussed, while that preference still governs how the correction is made. Distinguishing what someone wants from what they are entitled to decide is most of the judgement here.
questions.mindset: Honour a request about how something is handled without treating it as permission to leave the norm unaddressed.

questions.stem: Your most experienced platform engineer tells you she will resign unless a colleague is moved off the team. She describes months of him rewriting her work without discussion. He is unaware that there is any problem, and she has never raised it with him. She is two-thirds of the way through work that only she fully understands, and she wants an answer by the end of the week. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Decline to decide it on the terms offered, get the actual issue raised and worked through with him, and be honest with her about what you can and cannot promise by Friday.
options.rationale: The conduct she describes has never been tested by being raised, so no fair decision about either person is available yet. Being straight about the deadline respects her without accepting the framing.

options.text: Move him off the team, since losing her would cost the project far more.
options.rationale: It prices a decision about two people by which of them is harder to replace, and removes someone who has never been told there was a problem or given any chance to change.

options.text: Tell her the request cannot be met and ask her to reconsider her position.
options.rationale: It answers the ultimatum and ignores the months of conduct behind it, so the substance goes unexamined and she is left with the choice she arrived with.

options.text: Move her to another team so that the platform work can continue under someone else.
options.rationale: It relocates the person who raised the problem, which reads unmistakably as a penalty for raising it, and it also loses the knowledge you were trying to protect.

questions.explanation: An ultimatum sets terms as well as raising an issue, and accepting the terms decides the matter by leverage rather than by merit, which is unfair to whoever has less of it. The described conduct may well be serious, but it has never been put to the person doing it, so there is nothing yet to judge and no chance has been given to change. The honest response separates the substance, which deserves proper attention, from the deadline, which cannot be met without prejudging it.
questions.mindset: Take the grievance seriously and the terms of the ultimatum not at all.

questions.stem: Two suppliers on your stadium refurbishment each claim the other caused six weeks of standing time. Resolving entitlement properly means an independent review of both programmes, taking four weeks and occupying your commercial lead. The opening date is fixed by an events contract and three weeks of float remain. Your sponsor has told you to park the dispute and deliver. What should the project manager do?

options.text: Separate entitlement from delivery: preserve the records and reserve both parties' positions in writing now, agree that the review happens after opening, and secure both suppliers' agreement to continue working meanwhile.
options.rationale: It defers the resolution without losing the ability to resolve it, and it converts the sponsor's instruction into something that survives contact with a claim six months later.

options.text: Park the dispute as instructed and take it up once the venue has opened.
options.rationale: Parking without preserving records or reserving positions means the later review has little to work from, and both parties will by then have reconstructed accounts that favour them.

options.text: Run the independent review now, since entitlement is impossible to establish once the sequence is over.
options.rationale: It spends four weeks and the commercial lead against three weeks of float, trading a dispute about the past for a certain failure of a contractual opening date.

options.text: Split the six weeks of standing time equally between the two suppliers to close it quickly.
options.rationale: It buys speed with a settlement that neither party's evidence supports, and an arbitrary split gives both of them a reason to reopen it later with the same records intact.

questions.explanation: Disputes about entitlement and commitments about delivery run on different clocks, and the mistake is to assume that one must be sacrificed for the other. Deferring a resolution is legitimate project management; losing the ability to resolve it later is not, and the difference lies entirely in whether records are preserved and positions formally reserved at the time. A sponsor's instruction to park something is properly read as an instruction about sequence rather than about abandonment.
questions.mindset: Deferring a dispute is legitimate only if you preserve the means of settling it later.

questions.stem: You are settling a contract variation for additional ground works. Your quantity surveyor has authority to pay up to £84,000 and privately expects to settle nearer £70,000. The contractor's commercial manager has told you he cannot go below £62,000 and has opened by asking for £91,000. Work out whether a settlement is available on these figures, and identify what the £70,000 and £91,000 figures actually are.

blanks.label: Width of the overlap between the two parties' acceptable ranges, in £
blanks.rationale: Your side accepts anything up to £84,000 and the contractor accepts anything from £62,000 upward, so every figure between the two is acceptable to both: 84,000 − 62,000 gives £22,000 of overlap.

blanks.label: Amount by which the contractor's opening ask exceeds your surveyor's authority, in £
blanks.rationale: £91,000 less £84,000 is £7,000. An opening figure sitting outside the other side's authority proves only that the opening cannot be accepted as it stands, not that no settlement exists.

blanks.label: In negotiation terms, what the £70,000 expectation and the £91,000 ask are — the parties' limits or their openings
blanks.rationale: Neither figure is a limit: one is a private expectation and the other an opening ask. Treating an opening as a limit is what makes negotiators conclude too early that there is nothing to be had.

questions.explanation: A settlement is available whenever the parties' true limits overlap, and those limits are almost never the numbers either side says out loud. Establishing whether an overlap exists before arguing about where within it to land tells you whether you are negotiating or wasting everyone's time, and it stops an aggressive opening being mistaken for an impasse. The reverse error is just as costly: assuming an overlap that does not exist and conceding steadily into it.
questions.mindset: Work out whether the parties' limits overlap before arguing about the number, because openings are not limits.

questions.stem: You run a product team split between Osaka, Rotterdam and Bristol, and you have begun to notice that the sites express disagreement in very different ways from one another. Two observations from this month's joint planning sessions are set out below, and each invites a conclusion about what you are actually seeing. Complete each sentence with the conclusion that fits. One choice is not used.

prompts.text: Your Osaka colleagues have never openly rejected a proposal in a joint planning session, but three commitments made in those sessions have quietly gone undelivered. The project manager should conclude that
A Rotterdam engineer told the same session that the integration plan was simply wrong, then worked to it exactly as agreed once the decision was taken. The project manager should conclude that

options.text: disagreement is being expressed, and the session is not a place where it can be heard
options.rationale: Unanimous agreement followed by undelivered commitments is dissent in a form the meeting does not capture. The defect is in the channel rather than in the colleagues' candour or their reliability.

options.text: the objection was about the plan and the working relationship is intact
options.rationale: Blunt disagreement followed by compliance with the decision is task conflict handled openly. Reading the manner as hostility mistakes directness for a relationship problem and would penalise exactly the behaviour you want.

options.text: the team as a whole lacks the safety to disagree at all
options.rationale: Not used. It is directly contradicted by the second situation and too sweeping for the first, where disagreement is being expressed clearly enough, just not inside the meeting.

questions.explanation: Dissent takes different forms in different settings, and a project manager who recognises only the loud form will read compliant silence as agreement and blunt objection as conflict, getting both backwards. The reliable indicator is what happens to the commitments afterwards rather than how the room sounded at the time. Where disagreement is not surfacing in a forum, the useful assumption is that the forum is wrong for those people rather than that the people are difficult.
questions.mindset: Read dissent by what happens to the commitments afterwards, not by how loud the room was.
